detailed_summary: This paper (Part II of a two-part study) extends an optimal-control framework for designing high-fidelity controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons, previously developed in Part I to suppress intrinsic and decoherence-induced errors, by now incorporating parameter uncertainties. The authors classify uncertainties into two categories: those perturbing off-diagonal coupling strengths (coupling-strength errors) and those perturbing diagonal detunings (anharmonicities and zero-flux qubit frequencies). They identify distinct suppression mechanisms for each class. Coupling errors are mitigated via dynamical decoupling generated by strong detuning modulation; for a 30-ns gate this reduces coupling error to 6.21×10⁻⁷ and tolerates coupling-strength uncertainties up to 2π×4 MHz while keeping total infidelity below 10⁻³. Detuning errors are minimized near a symmetric-detuning operating point that balances two dominant leakage-mediated interactions; a 24-ns gate near this point tolerates individual uncertainties up to 2π×5 MHz in each relevant diagonal parameter under the same infidelity threshold. The authors then optimize gate performance under realistic conditions where intrinsic errors, decoherence, and parameter uncertainties coexist, across six representative stages of progressively improving hardware performance, yielding stage-specific controls with lower infidelity and greater robustness. The work is positioned as a practical route to balancing speed, fidelity, and robustness while reducing characterization and recalibration overhead in large-scale superconducting processors.
key_contributions: A classification of parameter uncertainties into off-diagonal (coupling-strength) and diagonal (detuning, anharmonicity, zero-flux frequency) classes, with distinct, physically motivated suppression mechanisms identified for each.

Demonstration that strong detuning modulation induces dynamical decoupling that suppresses coupling-strength errors, achieving coupling error of 6.21×10⁻⁷ for a 30-ns gate and tolerating coupling uncertainties up to 2π×4 MHz at infidelity below 10⁻³.

Identification of a symmetric-detuning operating point that balances two dominant leakage-mediated interactions, enabling a 24-ns gate to tolerate individual diagonal-parameter uncertainties up to 2π×5 MHz at the same infidelity threshold.

Stage-specific control optimization across six representative hardware-performance stages where intrinsic errors, decoherence, and parameter uncertainties coexist, yielding lower infidelity and improved robustness.

A practical framework (with Part I) for co-optimizing speed, fidelity, and robustness, reducing the need for exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration in large-scale superconducting processors.
methodology_analysis: The approach builds on the optimal-control framework of the companion paper (Part I), which designs CZ gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons while suppressing intrinsic and decoherence-induced errors. Here the control problem is augmented to include parameter uncertainties, which are partitioned by their effect on the Hamiltonian: off-diagonal coupling-strength perturbations versus diagonal detuning perturbations (anharmonicities and zero-flux frequencies). Rather than treating all uncertainties uniformly, the authors exploit the structure of each error class to design targeted suppression. For coupling errors, they rely on strong modulation of the detuning to induce an effective dynamical-decoupling behavior that averages out coupling-strength fluctuations. For detuning errors, they analyze the leakage-mediated interactions and locate a symmetric-detuning operating point where the two dominant contributions balance, minimizing sensitivity. The optimization is then repeated under realistic composite conditions—intrinsic errors, decoherence, and parameter uncertainties together—across six staged hardware-performance scenarios, producing stage-specific pulse controls. The methodology is thus a structured, physics-informed robust-control design rather than a generic worst-case optimization, which is a notable methodological choice.
results_analysis: The headline quantitative results are: for a 30-ns gate, coupling error is suppressed to 6.21×10⁻⁷, with tolerance to coupling-strength uncertainties up to 2π×4 MHz while total gate infidelity remains below 10⁻³. For detuning-type errors, a 24-ns gate operated near the symmetric-detuning point tolerates individual uncertainties up to 2π×5 MHz in each relevant diagonal parameter under the same 10⁻³ infidelity threshold. These numbers indicate that the robust-control design preserves fast gate times (24–30 ns) while maintaining error budgets compatible with fault-tolerant-relevant thresholds, though the 10⁻³ threshold itself is above the commonly cited ~10⁻⁴ surface-code target, so the reported tolerances should be read as robustness margins at a moderate fidelity level rather than at fault-tolerance-grade fidelities. The staged optimization across six hardware-performance regimes is reported to yield lower infidelity and greater robustness than non-stage-specific controls, supporting the practical claim that controls can be tailored to expected hardware quality. The paper does not, in the provided text, give explicit infidelity values for the staged results, so the magnitude of improvement is asserted rather than quantified here.
strengths: The uncertainty classification into off-diagonal versus diagonal perturbations is physically insightful and leads to distinct, well-motivated suppression mechanisms rather than a one-size-fits-all robust-control treatment.
Concrete, quantitative robustness results (6.21×10⁻⁷ coupling error; 2π×4 MHz and 2π×5 MHz tolerances at 10⁻³ infidelity) for fast 24–30 ns gates provide directly usable design targets.

The staged optimization across six hardware-performance regimes addresses realistic coexistence of intrinsic errors, decoherence, and parameter uncertainty, improving practical relevance over idealized single-error studies.
The framework's emphasis on reducing characterization and recalibration burden is well aligned with the operational needs of large-scale superconducting processors.
limitations: The robustness thresholds are quoted at a total infidelity below 10⁻³, which is above fault-tolerance-relevant targets (~10⁻⁴), so the practical significance for error-corrected operation is not fully established in the provided text.

The analysis is restricted to directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons and CZ gates; generalization to other couplers (e.g., tunable couplers), other gate types, or multi-qubit contexts is not demonstrated.

The staged results are described qualitatively (lower infidelity, greater robustness) without explicit numerical infidelity values in the available text, limiting independent assessment of the improvement magnitude.
connections_to_research: This work sits squarely within quantum physics and quantum information science, specifically superconducting-qubit control and error mitigation. For a researcher interested in quantum physics broadly, it offers a concrete case study in how Hamiltonian structure (off-diagonal coupling versus diagonal detuning) dictates error-suppression strategy—an idea with analogues in dynamical decoupling and robust quantum control more generally. The use of detuning modulation to induce effective dynamical decoupling connects to foundational quantum-control concepts, while the leakage-mediated symmetric operating point illustrates how multi-level (transmon) physics shapes gate design. The staged, uncertainty-aware optimization also speaks to the broader challenge of scaling quantum processors, making it relevant to both device-level and algorithm-level quantum information research.
overall_assessment: This is a technically solid, well-structured extension of a companion optimal-control framework, with genuine novelty in its classification-driven treatment of parameter uncertainties and in the identification of a symmetric-detuning operating point that balances leakage-mediated interactions. The quantitative robustness results for fast 24–30 ns CZ gates are useful and specific, and the staged optimization adds practical value. Its main weaknesses are the moderate 10⁻³ infidelity threshold relative to fault-tolerance targets, the narrow scope (directly coupled tunable transmons, CZ only), and the qualitative reporting of staged improvements in the available text. Overall, it is a valuable contribution to robust superconducting-gate design, best regarded as a practical engineering framework whose fault-tolerance-grade performance remains to be demonstrated.
